Medical Assistant Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)

A medical assistant resume has to do two jobs at once. Clinics want hands that can run vitals, phlebotomy, and EKGs without a second thought. The same clinics want a front desk that keeps the schedule full, the insurance verified, and the chart complete. One resume that proves only one half will lose to one that proves both.

This guide gives you a full annotated example for a certified medical assistant in a busy family practice, a section-by-section breakdown, and the mistakes that cost interviews.

The example below is fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern that works: what you did, at what volume, and with what result.

Quick answer: A medical assistant resume should include a summary naming your certification and setting; a clinical block with the procedures you can run, such as vitals, phlebotomy, and EKGs; an administrative block covering scheduling, insurance verification, and the electronic health record you use; and experience bullets pairing each duty with a count, such as patients seen per day.

Key Takeaways

  • Lead with certification and setting — CMA, and the clinic type and size you worked in.
  • Prove both halves: clinical procedures with volumes, and administrative work with counts.
  • Name the electronic health record you can use on day one: Epic, Cerner, or eClinicalWorks.
  • Every experience bullet pairs a duty with a count: patients per day, draws per week, or errors caught.
  • Keep the file single-column with standard headings and real text, so applicant tracking systems parse it cleanly.

What Clinic Hiring Managers Actually Look For

Talk to a practice manager and you will not hear “compassionate team player.” You will hear:

  • Certification, stated plainly. CMA, RMA, or CCMA, plus BLS and any phlebotomy credential. An uncertified applicant goes in a different pile in most clinics.
  • Clinical volume. Patients roomed per day, draws per week, EKGs per shift. A medical assistant who handled 28 patients a day in a busy practice is a safer hire than one who lists procedures without numbers.
  • Administrative proof. Scheduling, insurance verification, referrals, and prior authorizations, with the counts that show the desk ran smoothly. A clinic loses money on every unverified visit and every empty slot.
  • EHR fluency. Epic, Cerner, or eClinicalWorks, named exactly. Charting is half the job, and a hire who needs weeks of EHR training costs the clinic a month of productivity.
  • Accuracy under pressure. Vitals charted correctly, specimens labelled right the first time, referrals sent without a missing form. One mislabelled specimen can cost a clinic a patient.

If your resume reads like a duties list — all responsibilities, no volumes — it will lose to one that reads like a shift record.

Medical Assistant Resume Example (Annotated)

Below is a complete example for a certified medical assistant in a family practice. It’s fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern hiring managers respond to: what you did, the volume, and the result.

SOFIA RAMIREZ, CMA
Houston, TX · (713) 555-0182 · sofia.ramirez@email.com

SUMMARY
Certified Medical Assistant (CMA) with 5 years in family practice and urgent care, including 3 years at a 6-provider clinic seeing 120+ patients a day. Room 28 patients daily, run phlebotomy and EKGs, and keep the Epic chart current with zero documentation errors in the last year. BLS-certified; phlebotomy certified.

CERTIFICATIONS & CLINICAL SKILLS
Certified Medical Assistant (CMA) · Basic Life Support (BLS), current · Phlebotomy certification · Vitals & EKGs · Injections & immunizations · Specimen collection & labelling · Wound care assistance · Spirometry · Epic EHR · eClinicalWorks

SKILLS
Patient intake · Vital signs · Phlebotomy · EKGs · Injections · Specimen handling · Scheduling · Insurance verification · Referrals & prior authorizations · Epic EHR · Charting · Sterile technique · Patient education · Bilingual English/Spanish

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

Certified Medical Assistant — Riverside Family Practice, Houston, TX | 2022–Present

  • Room 28 patients a day across 6 providers, taking vitals, updating histories, and preparing charts so providers start on time
  • Draw 40+ blood samples a week with a first-stick success rate above 95%, and run EKGs and spirometry on the same visit where ordered
  • Verify insurance for every scheduled visit the day before, cutting same-day eligibility surprises from 6 a week to fewer than 1
  • Cut the clinic’s no-show rate from 14% to 9% by running the reminder calls and filling cancelled slots from the waitlist the same day
  • Keep Epic charts current with zero documentation errors in the last year, closing every chart the same day the patient was seen

Medical Assistant — QuickCare Urgent Care, Houston, TX | 2020–2022

  • Triaged walk-in patients in a 12-bed urgent care, rooming 35+ patients per shift during flu season
  • Ran point-of-care testing, including rapid strep and flu swabs, and labelled every specimen correctly across 2 years
  • Handled front-desk intake for evening shifts, scheduling follow-ups and processing referrals for 3 providers
  • Trained 4 new medical assistants on the clinic’s intake flow, EKG setup, and specimen handling

Medical Assistant Extern — Bayou City Pediatrics, Houston, TX | 2020 (160 hours)

  • Completed a 160-hour externship, rooming 15+ pediatric patients a day and assisting with immunizations
  • Learned Epic charting on live visits, with every chart reviewed and signed off by the supervising provider

EDUCATION
Medical Assistant Diploma — Houston Community College, 2020 · CMA exam passed 2020

Why it works: the summary leads with the certification and the two numbers clinics check — patients per day and documentation accuracy. Every bullet pairs a duty with a count, and the climb from extern to a 6-provider practice shows the whole progression.

Section-by-Section Breakdown

Summary: certification and setting first, then volume

“CMA,” “6-provider clinic,” “28 patients daily,” “zero documentation errors in the last year” — the certification answers the eligibility question; the volume answers the competence question. If you are newly certified, lead with the externship and the certification instead.

Experience: volumes, not responsibilities

“Assisted with patient care” is a responsibility; “room 28 patients a day and draw 40+ blood samples a week” is proof of capacity. The strongest bullets show a number that moved because of work you did.

Certifications: exact letters, current status

List the credential exactly as it appears on the certificate, with the expiry where it matters. Hiring managers screen on these letters before reading experience.

Medical Assistant Skills & ATS Keywords

Mirror the posting’s language exactly: “phlebotomy” vs “venipuncture” matters:

  • Clinical: vital signs, phlebotomy, venipuncture, EKG, ECG, injections, immunizations, specimen collection, wound care, spirometry, triage, sterile technique
  • Administrative: scheduling, insurance verification, prior authorizations, referrals, patient intake, charting, medical records, front desk
  • Systems: Epic, Cerner, eClinicalWorks, electronic health record, EHR, patient portal, point-of-care testing
  • Credentials: CMA, RMA, CCMA, BLS, phlebotomy certification, medical assistant diploma

Check your resume against a free ATS scan — for example, Cvyon's ATS grader — before you apply. Clinics screen resumes through applicant tracking systems, and multi-column layouts and text-in-graphics are the usual parsing killers. Start from a clean template in Cvyon's template gallery, or the role page for medical assistants. Note the difference from the nursing role: nurses hold a nursing license and own assessment and care planning, while medical assistants work under a physician or nurse practitioner across clinical and administrative tasks.

5 Mistakes That Cost Medical Assistants Interviews

  1. Hiding the certification. A resume that buries CMA or RMA at the bottom forces the reader to hunt for the one line that decides the pile. Put it in the summary and in its own block.
  2. Listing duties instead of volumes. “Assisted with patient care” is a job description; “room 28 patients a day and draw 40+ samples a week” is capacity. Lead with volumes.
  3. Claiming a credential you do not hold. “CMA” when you have never sat the exam is a misrepresentation clinics verify. State it honestly: “CMA exam scheduled” or “CMA candidate.”
  4. No EHR named. Epic, Cerner, or eClinicalWorks — a resume without an EHR reads as if charting was never done. Name the system and the years you used it.
  5. One generic resume for every clinic. Tailor the summary and first bullets to the setting: volume and triage speed for urgent care, continuity and chart accuracy for family practice, paediatric patience for a children’s clinic.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should be included in a medical assistant resume?

A summary naming your certification and the setting you worked in; a clinical block with the procedures you can run, such as vitals, phlebotomy, and EKGs; an administrative block covering scheduling, insurance verification, and the electronic health record you use; and experience bullets pairing each duty with a count, such as patients seen per day or forms processed without errors.

How do I show clinical skills on a medical assistant resume?

Name each procedure you can run on day one: vitals, phlebotomy, injections, EKGs, spirometry, and specimen handling, with the volume where it proves competence, such as 40+ draws a week. Add the setting, because a busy urgent-care clinic and a quiet specialty office ask for different proof.

What certifications should a medical assistant list on a resume?

List the ones you actually hold: Certified Medical Assistant (CMA), Registered Medical Assistant (RMA), Certified Clinical Medical Assistant (CCMA), and Basic Life Support (BLS) are the common ones, plus phlebotomy certification where you have it. Never claim a credential you do not hold; clinics verify before the first shift.

How long should a medical assistant resume be?

One page for most medical assistants, including experienced ones. Two pages only if you carry a career across genuinely different settings, such as urgent care, a specialty practice, and a hospital, that each need space; even then keep the certification and the strongest numbers on page one.

What is the difference between a medical assistant and a nurse on a resume?

A medical assistant works under a physician or nurse practitioner and splits time between clinical tasks, such as vitals and phlebotomy, and administrative work, such as scheduling and insurance. A nurse holds a nursing license and owns assessment and care planning. State the scope you actually held, and never claim nursing duties you did not perform.

Do I need experience to get a medical assistant job?

Most clinics hire newly certified medical assistants, especially from an externship. An externship counts as experience if you name the clinic, the weeks, and what you did: patients roomed per day, procedures assisted, and the EHR you used. Lead with the externship and the certification, not with unrelated jobs.
